decision_status_reason: The findings of the LED NIR kidney study cannot be quoted as proof that a sensor is ready for intraoperative tumor boundary guidance in live surgery. The cited study is a proof-of-concept on ex vivo samples; in vivo validation, clinical studies, and regulatory approval are required for patient use, which are outside the scope of this technical assessment. The appropriate next step is a laboratory feasibility study using the intended sensor and relevant tissue types.

clarification_questions.question: What is the intended tumor type and anatomical site for boundary detection?
Can you provide details of your proposed sensor design and its compatibility with surgical workflow?
Will the sensor be used in direct contact with tissue, or at a distance? What are the sterility and cleaning requirements?
What are the expected optical properties (scattering, absorption) of the target tissue compared to kidney tissue?
What reference method or clinical standard will be used to validate tumor boundary detection?

recommendations.rationale: Diffuse reflectance NIR spectroscopy with a fiber probe is supported for ex vivo tumor/normal discrimination and is the basis of the cited kidney study; it is worth laboratory testing on the intended tissue type.
recommendations.applies_when: The tissue type is similar in optical properties to kidney and the sensor can be adapted for the surgical workflow.

citations.supports: NIR diffuse reflectance is promising for tumor/normal discrimination in tissue.

recommendations.rationale: Combining NIR with MIR-ATR or fluorescence may improve boundary detection in heterogeneous tissues; this is supported for ex vivo tissue classification and margin recognition.
recommendations.applies_when: The tissue is heterogeneous or the NIR-only approach is insufficient for robust discrimination.

citations.supports: Multispectral approaches (NIR, MIR-ATR, fluorescence) are used for tumor margin recognition.
Combining fluorescence and IR improves tumor margin detection.

measurement_concept.summary: A laboratory feasibility study should be performed using the intended sensor (or a close prototype) on ex vivo samples of the target tissue, comparing NIR (and optionally multispectral) fiber probe measurements at the intended measurement geometry to histopathological reference. In vivo or intraoperative use is not supported without further validation.
measurement_concept.fiber_link_note: Standard Vis-NIR silica fibers are suitable for NIR diffuse reflectance in the 900–1500 nm range as in the cited study.

citations.supports: The cited study used a fiber-coupled NIR diffuse reflectance probe with LEDs at 0.94, 1.17, 1.30, and 1.44 um.
Further studies are needed for other organs and in vivo use.

risks.risk: Ex vivo or in vitro results may not translate to in vivo or intraoperative performance due to differences in tissue properties, environment, and measurement conditions.
risks.mitigation: Conduct laboratory feasibility studies on fresh ex vivo samples of the intended tissue type, followed by controlled in vivo validation before any clinical use.

citations.supports: Spectra of frozen/thawed biopsies can differ from real-life in vivo measurements.

feasibility_plan.objective: To determine whether the proposed NIR (or multispectral) fiber-optic sensor can reliably discriminate tumor from normal tissue in the intended anatomical context, using ex vivo samples.
samples_or_process_states: Fresh ex vivo samples of the intended tumor type and anatomical site
Representative normal tissue from the same site
reference_measurements: Histopathological assessment of tumor boundaries (gold standard)
comparisons: Comparison of NIR-only and multispectral (if available) approaches
steps: Define the sensor configuration and measurement geometry for the intended tissue.
Collect ex vivo tissue samples representing tumor and normal regions.
Acquire NIR (and optionally multispectral) spectra at defined locations using the sensor.
Process data using chemometric classification models (e.g., PLS-DA).
Compare sensor-based discrimination to histopathological reference.
Assess robustness across tissue heterogeneity and sample variability.
feasibility_plan.go_no_go_basis: Go/no-go is based on the sensor's ability to discriminate tumor from normal tissue with accuracy meeting client-defined acceptance targets, as validated against histopathology. No clinical or in vivo claims are made at this stage.

premise_checks.finding: Research and proof-of-concept results are a reason to test a method, not proof that a different set-up is ready for the intended use.
